note_tweet.text:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, I witnessed, through Japanese television broadcasts, the immense suffering and loss of life unfolding across the world. Seeing so many people die, day after day, left me emotionally overwhelmed. I felt a profound sense of helplessness, painfully aware of how little one person could do in the face of such widespread human suffering. Since then, I have found myself unable to watch conventional television broadcasts.

I also sometimes find it deeply difficult to watch reports of capital punishment, violent crimes, and the lives destroyed by acts of cruelty. Whether I see victims who have been killed or survivors whose lives have been irreversibly changed, there are moments when the weight of what I witness leaves me speechless.

Perhaps this is because I, too, am a victim of crime.

For me, these are not merely stories in the news. They touch something deeply personal within me. Behind every headline is a human life, a person with a history, relationships, hopes, and a future that may have been taken away or forever altered.

I believe that the ability to recognize another person's suffering is not a weakness, but an essential expression of our humanity. Yet compassion can also be painful, especially when we are confronted with suffering we cannot prevent or injustices we cannot undo.

I may not be able to save every life, heal every wound, or change every tragedy. But I never want to become indifferent to the value of a human life simply because the suffering of others is too painful to bear.

Perhaps our humanity is revealed not only by what we have the power to change, but also by what we refuse to stop caring about, even when we feel powerless.
